posts.author: a_k
posts.content_md:
Hello everyone. 

After a lot of struggling I finally managed to consistently get bright and clear holograms with MBDCG. Three different gelatines were tried and only one of them works. The non-working gelatines were one supposed to be Rousselot Photo Gelatine and one local variety (Haenseler) bovine gelatine with a bloom strength of 128-192 and an isoelectric point of pH 4.7-5.6. The latter produced some but irritating results.

The only working variety i found was Gelita photo gelatine.

A Sony SLD1239JL-54 658nm/100mW Laserdiode was used at a power range between 20-35mW for the exposures. The wavelength of this LD is very close to the absorbtion maximum of MB.

Jeff's original MBDCG papers (applied optics, HI7) were the base for all attempts. TMG was replaced with Guanidine Carbonate, which is supposed to result in 2-3 times less sensitivity, and this equals to 100-150mJ/cm2. The exposure level i need for bright denisyuk holograms is 300-400mJ/cm2. And even this is only achieved after breathing upon the plates shorthly before exposure. The plates are a nice clear blue color before exposure.

Upon Jeffs suggestion i tried bleaching test with MB/GK/Gelatine but could not get any photo reaction, again, unless breathing upon the plates. 

So I assumed that the humidity level of the plates was too low and followed Jeffs suggestion and added 10% glycerine to the MBDCG mixtures. No improvement was achieved this way.

To get some better idea of the RH conditions i'm now using a hygrometer, freshly calibrated. The last batch of my plates was dried at 55% RH and used at 60%RH. 

In one of the papers Jeff discusses in some detail the dependency of sensitivity and RH. According to the numbers given there it's not too likely that the small deviation of my RH conditions from the ones suggested would cause a threefold lessened sensitivity. And also the fact that the (as I learnt in the meantime) large amount of 10% glycerine did not lead to an improvement suggests some other cause for the small sensitivity. Also the fact that even 2400mJ/cm2 does not result in anything (without breathing) suggests to me that the (slightly off) RH is not the problem. How dry a plate has to be for being that blind?

As the light source i'm using far better fits the absorbtion maximum of MB than the laser employed in Jeff's text, (Ruby 694nm) i was actually expecting to need a substantially lower exposure level and not one several times higher.

A few of my test holograms were broadband but most are narrowband and show a very nice golden-copper colour. As TMG was replaced 1:1 weightwise with GK i would have thought to get some color closer to green. The good thing about this is that i can add some more GK and thus enhance sensitivity and still get some visible color despite the blue-shift.

I don't know if adding more GK would also require to add more potassium chromate and MB to keep the proportions equal. Any ideas about this?

Any ideas about possible causes for the way too low sensitivity i'm experiencing and why i have to employ my breath before each exposure? The more i think about it the less likely it seems to me that RH is the cause. It's more like the humidity is more or less ok, and that the "sensitivity boost" triggered by the breath masks away some other problem.

What are other's experienced exposure levels with MBDCG and maybe in conjunction with Guanidine Carbonate?

Thanks, 

Ahmet.

posts.content_md:
A TEC centered on maxims MAX1968 peltier controller is being built but far from finished yet. In the meantime i'm using two LM317 circuits. One of them is a simple adjustable "precision" current controller for the LD. It is fed by another LM317 circuit with just about the voltage level required to keep the heat produced at a very low level. The chaining of this two circuits proved to be quite usable. 

At first I was using batteries as power source but as this seemed to be unnecessary precaution i'm using a switched 220V -> 12V DC converter now.

The laser module is strapped onto cooling fins. It has been quite hot here lately and the room temp was 31°C at times. As a result I was getting less power from the LD. So i had the crazy idea of strapping a small CPU-cooler onto the cooling fins. I was not really expecting to get any results with this combination because of vibrations. Quite to my surprise i'm getting successful exposures longer than 6 minutes this way.

The LD has two quite broad stable operating current levels. One around 20mW the other at 30-35mw at room temp. For tests i actively cooled the diode down to about 12°C and could observe that the two usable operating levels were shifted towards more power. That way it was possible to operate the LD at higher currents and obtaining up to 65mW with similar light quality as the 30mW and room temp.

I'm pretty sure that this LD can be operated at the nominal power of 100mW if sufficiently cooled. But then condensing humidity gets problematic. So I would assume that 65mW at about 14-15°C is a reasonable limit for using the Sony Diode.

Tom, thanks for the suggestions. Me to I was thinking about what is so special about my breath - it's not god's odem. I ruled out O2 because the breath expelled contains less of it than the surrounding air, the nitrogen level remains unchanged too.

As a test i placed some plates in a humidity saturated atmosphere before exposure but could not get any reaction to light out of them. So the higher humidity through breathing might be ruled out.

But the CO2 is much higher in the breath and i thought that maybe this could cause a drop of the pH. The succesful MBDCG solution has a pH of 9.5 by the way. This is the value I got when combining the Gelita gelatine with GK. No adjustment of the pH with an acid was necessary, because the value is in the range Jeff recommends (9-9.5) .

So I produced a glass with over a dozen test strips with differing pH between 8.2 and 10. The adjustment of pH was made with a 4% w/v soultion of boric acid. None of the strips showed any reaction to light without breathing. If it's the CO2 that's causing the different behaviour of plates, then its not only because it reduces the pH of the coating. I'll give your idea with the CO2 cartridges a try and report the outcome.

I even suspected the small temperature increase of the plates caused by the breath. But this seems to be an unlikely thing because the amount of energy involved is minimal and during the couple of minutes until exposure the plates would cool back to room temp.

During my MBDCG tests i had a lot of failures because of the gelatine used. The Gelita gelatine works to some degreee. Maybe it's the gelatine in the end that's responsible for the low sensitivity of my emulsion. I would love to test a gelatine that has been used by others with good results, but can't get the brands recommended by other forum members because they are simply not available here.

Dave, thanks for the kind words. I used an Osram 20W 10° halogen spot at a distance of about 3m from the plate for tho+se pictures. The holograms are brighter than the photos suggest, and i had to compress the images quite a bit to get below the 256K file size limit. I was very surprised about the extreme clarity of the holograms too. On one of the photos i could see really tiny details that i had not even noticed on the coins themselves.

MBDCG works, even with my very improvized setup. But at a needed light level of 300-400mJ one is quite limited to small test holograms of flat objects. I really hope to overcome this obstacle and try something more creative than coins

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
> **a_k:** Jeff's original MBDCG papers (applied optics, HI7) were the base for all attempts. TMG was replaced with Guanidine Carbonate, which is supposed to result in 2-3 times less sensitivity, and this equals to 100-150mJ/cm2. The exposure level i need for bright denisyuk holograms is 300-400mJ/cm2. The plates are a nice clear blue color before exposure.

If you don't have access to TMG, then it seems the benefit you're getting from guanidine carbonate is doubtful. I would suggest taking a look at two early papers by Kubota and others (Applied Optics 1976 and 1979). In the first one (Hologram formation with red light in methylene blue sensitized dichromated gelatin) they give the exposure level as follows:

"The energy required to obtain 80% diffraction efficiency is 150-400 mJ/cm2."

Perhaps more significant is the other paper called "Methods of increasing the sensitivity of methylene blue sensitized dichromated gelatin." They use the same film forumla as in the earlier paper, but got a further increase in sensitivity by either heating after expsoure, or by allowing a lapse of time after expsoure (i.e., an accelerated dark reaction by heating, or natural dark reaction by ageing). I think it would be of considerable benefit to rely on the dark reaction as much as possible, because MBDCG is so slow.

If you don't have either of the two papers, please send me a PM with your email address, and I will send you .pdf copies.

posts.author: jeff-blyth
posts.content_md:
Congratulations on your perseverance and results Ahmet.

My results and calcs were originally done with 633nm. HeNe---(The 694nm ruby pulsed stuff was just a proof of principle and no value should be put on the energy level, --the pulses were very variable in energy output as judged very crudely by the loudness of the bang from the capacitor discharges each time!). 

I suggested using glycerol as humectant because of its ease of procurement from local stores but a better humectant would be ethylene glycol (ethane diol ). 

I am not able to say whether the additional items put in ethylene glycol used as car anti-freeze would spoil things but ethylene glycol alone is exceptionally good at retaining moisture compared to the other poly alcohols. Could you get some pure ?.

(BTW the glycerol used in the ( “G307”) system from the 2006 Symposium paper is for a very different ball game involving reactions at 100C and some possible oxidation reaction from dichromate derivatives at acid pH levels. 

With regard to your point about balancing more guanidine carbonate with more chromate, --- no, that is not how the system works. The essence of the mechanism is primarily to get the MB to be bleached by the light and GC ( plenty of moisture 

is needed for this reaction to work well) however the bleached MB then gets oxidized by the chromate so rapidly that you don’t see it actually getting bleached in the first place. But you would or should see it bleach if you don’t add any chromate as you know and that bleaching reaction with light is THE rate determining step. The chromate reaction to restore the colour is not rate determining and adding more chromate may be detrimental.. 

Jeff

posts.content_md:
That white spot......a simple explanation?

Ahmet, if you take a reflection silver halide hologram on glass , chill it and then with the gelatin side unprotected you breathe heavily on it,

you get the classic red shift effect over most of the area . But that visible effect from say a green to red replay only lasts a few seconds (depending on room temperature and humidity) but over the final second or so of this visible effect of moisture swelling you get the original red shift shrinking away from the edges to a final circular patch of redness in the center. Now here you have a fringe structure on hardened gelatin that is demonstrating what must happen when you have a softer gelatin in your exposure set up that you have just breathed on prior to making your MBDCG. That last bit in the middle is still shrinking and destroying the fringe structure you are trying to make. So it finishes up as a dead white spot of jumbled up fringes after you have processed it.

Jeff

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Hey Jeff, that's interesting. I had not thought of it that way.

My line of thinking was as follows:

Back to my old philosophy of when we process a DCG hologram we are actually causing an effect or a change on the unexposed gelatin not the exposed gelatin. We are processing the unexposed areas. This is not to be confused with the "non object" areas.

I would suspect in his descriptions that the "springs" have broken in his object area. In what he describes as the non image part of the plate, there is exposure. In fact it averages as much exposure as the image area minus the object beam (full reference beam). Quite a bit of light. Now in the image area we have alternating no exposure and exposure. It is in these non exposure areas (destructive interference) where I suspect the problem. Those destrucive fringes are getting way less light then the non image area. The gelatin is soooo soft there that when it is swollen in the fixer/water, the loose bonds break apart due to swelling before the fixer can harden them into place. Thus on drying the destructive fringes collapse onto the constructive fringes. The gelatin in the destructive fringes is simply way to soft and underhardened.

This seems to be an intersting thought because in this case, no amont of additional exposure can remedy the problem. The destructive fringes will always recieve no light and be too soft. The only way I see on correcting this problem is to preharden or post harden the plate in such a way that the entire gelatin and more specifically the unexposed, destructive fringes get some crosslinking. If this theory is corret then either prior or after the exposure, if the hologram is exposed to the laser light while being held in the hand and being moved so no fringes are formed, the unexposed destructive fringe areas my get enough crosslinking to support the fringe structure. I would do it for about the same time as the exposure, or at least as long as it takes for the non image areas to become clear after processing.

That's my take anyway.

I came along a text by David I. Hitchcock ("The isoelectric point of a standard gelatine preparation" published July 20 1931, in "The journal of general Physiology"). Among other interesting stuff, a number of different methods for determining the isoelectric point of gelatin are presented in this paper.

The two methods i thought to be able to conduct with my primitive tools are:

- Measuring the level of opacity of the solution while scanning a pH range, when maximum scattering is found, it is the isoelectric point

 (this proved to be not practicable for me because i could not measure the opacity with the desired level of resolution. I would need to improve my tools first.)

- "the pH of of a pure solution of a simple ampholyte must lie between that of pure water and that of the isoelectric point of the ampholyte, approaching the latter figure as the concentration is increased."

I don't trust the number i got this way because it indicates that the rousselot gelatine had an isoelectric point around pH 5.47 but it was completely useless for MBDCG. The main difficulty with this method was the standard gelatine preparation. It's basically washing the gelatine with cold distilled water several times to remove foreign ions. But ideally the water used for the washing should have a pH close to the pH of the gelatin at its isoelectric point in order to remove last traces of electrolytes.

Jeff, do you know of a simple way of changing the isoelectric point of a gelatine from, let's say pH 9 to pH 5? I know that this value is determined by the production method, but can it be lowered afterwards?

How were your results with Dr. Oetker gelatine and are you still using it? DId you notice any change with different batches of that gelatine?

I have temporarily stopped doing MBDCG to be able to spend more time at researching home made AgBr plates. There are differences with types of gelatin, but they are not big in MBDCG. If you have enough of a certain type, stick with it. If it works it works and try to refine what you can get with it.

> Adding TEA might be a good thing. I'll try that for sure. My limiting factor for further tests is a suitable gelatine at the moment.

I don't know if adding TEA is a good idea or not. I know TMG is supposed to work much better and a lot of research has been done using TEA with MBDCG without many good results. I am sure Jeff can give more insight on the idea of using TEA. But.... holography is a strange beast. Often just trying things that might seem illogical at times will have surprizing results. And the way to get good results is to keep trying every trick you can think of. Using TEA alone as a electron donor does not much good with MBDCG. But it does help retain water and who knows, perhaps in combination with your carbon TMG it might surprize us and do something unexpected.

> . I did follow many your threads and could extract quite a bit of useful information from them. And i'll try your express drying method with cold/warm hair dryer. How long by the way did this treatment take to sufficiently simulate the dark reaktion?

Using a cold hair drier before exposure helps a lot to equalize the humidity of the plate with the humidity of the lab. This helps prevent movement of the emulsion during exposure. It helps to dry a plate that has just been coated with a hair drier because it just speeds up the experiment so much and there is a bigger chance of still having a lot of TMG in the plate.

I am still not sure if the hot hair drier after exposure helps much because I have never observed any dark reaction without hair drying. And the times I got good results with alternating hot/cold drying before developing could be because of pure coincidence. I just kept on doing it to keep one variable constant.

> What gelatine are you using and what are the the exposure levels it takes for you to get nice holograms?

With normal TMG MBDCG any exposure above 40mJ works fine with a diode at 658nm. A HeNe at 632nm needs a little more because the MB absorbs less at this wavelength. I found no difference in sensitivity with different types of gelatin. If your lab is very humid, you will find that with some types of gelatin the plate will loose it's blue colour before exposure has started. That is bad. And that is what most of my tests were for at the time. Now I have my lab humidity and temperature controlled and there is no such problem anymore. Just make sure that the humidity stays below 65% and the temperature stays above 20C and you'll be fine.

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
> With normal TMG MBDCG any exposure above 40mJ works fine with a diode at 658nm.

Just to expand on this: It really is difficult to over expose MBDCG. If you expose longer, you can still get a similar result by preswelling with warmer water. Often it is easier to get an even coloured narrow band hologram with longer exposures. When exposures get longer it seems as if the water temperatures where you start to see a narrow band hologram and the temperature where the hologram starts to be broad band and the temperature where you reach the yield point are further apart. Exposing at 40mJ and developing at 26C seems to give an optimal combination for reproducible golden broad band holograms. I have found that this combination works with nearly any type of gelatin of similar bloom.
